summary: This standards-track document defines a new TLV for MPLS LSP Ping so it can check connectivity of Point-to-Multipoint pseudowires. LSP Ping is a widely used operations and maintenance tool in MPLS networks. The new TLV lets operators test these multi-receiver pseudowires with the same familiar tool.

plainLanguage.summary: Ping checks if a friend can hear you. This adds a way to check that a message sent to many friends along a branching path really reaches each one.

subtitle: How to ping a point-to-multipoint pseudowire and check that every leaf router can be reached.

tldr.problem: Operators had LSP Ping for checking MPLS paths, but it had no way to say which point-to-multipoint pseudowire (P2MP PW) was being tested at the leaf routers.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a new P2MP Pseudowire sub-TLV, carried in the Target FEC Stack TLV of an echo request. It holds an Attachment Group Identifier and the root's IP address, and it is sent over the P2MP LSP with one of two encapsulations.
tldr.outcome: Operators can run the familiar LSP Ping against P2MP pseudowires. IANA assigned sub-TLV type 37 for it, and the Standards Track document adds no new security considerations beyond RFC 6425.

today: RFC 8339 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2018. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the definition of the P2MP Pseudowire sub-TLV for LSP Ping.

sections.title: Why P2MP Pseudowires Need Their Own Ping
sections.content:
A Point-to-Multipoint (P2MP) Pseudowire emulates the essential attributes of a unidirectional P2MP service, such as P2MP ATM, over a Public Switched Network. It is carried over a P2MP MPLS LSP. Requirements are in RFC 7338, BGP signaling is in RFC 7117 and LDP signaling for single segment P2MP PWs is in RFC 8338.

Data-plane failures on P2MP MPLS LSPs are already covered by RFC 6425. This document adds the missing piece for pseudowires riding on those LSPs: a way to tell the receiving Leaf PE which P2MP PW is under test. Multi-segment pseudowires are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Many pipes can share one big branching pipe. When you test it, you also have to say which small pipe you mean, or the far end will not know what to check.

sections.title: Tree Arrangements for P2MP PWs
sections.content:
Many P2MP PWs can share the same P2MP MPLS LSP. The RFC names several ways the LSP can be used.

  • Aggregate P2MP Tree: many PWs share one LSP. This needs an upstream-assigned label so the Leaf PE (L-PE) can link traffic to a VPN or VPLS instance.
  • Inclusive P2MP Tree: the LSP carries only one VPN or VPLS service instance, so the LSP label alone identifies the service.
  • Selective P2MP Tree: each multicast group in a VPN or VPLS instance gets its own unique P2MP LSP.
  • Aggregate Selective P2MP Tree: traffic for a set of multicast groups from different VPN or VPLS instances shares one P2MP LSP.

The LSPs are set up with P2MP RSVP-TE (RFC 4875) or Multipoint LDP (RFC 6388).
sections.plainLanguage: Some branching pipes carry water for one house, and some are shared by many houses. Each way needs its own labelling so the right water goes to the right tap.

sections.title: The P2MP Pseudowire Sub-TLV
sections.content:
The new P2MP Pseudowire sub-TLV goes inside the Target FEC Stack TLV of the echo request. The originator, at the Root PE (R-PE), adds it to tell the receiver at the L-PE which P2MP PW is being tested.

It has an AGI Type, an AGI Length and an AGI Value, followed by an IP Addr Len and the Originating Router's IP address. The Attachment Group Identifier (AGI), as described in Section 3.4.2 of RFC 4446, identifies the VPLS instance. The originating address is the IPv4 or IPv6 address of the P2MP PW root, and the IP Addr Len field determines the address family.

The label stack depends on the tree. For Inclusive and Selective P2MP Trees the echo request uses the P2MP MPLS LSP label. For Aggregate Inclusive and Aggregate Selective trees it uses the stack [P2MP MPLS LSP label, upstream assigned P2MP PW label], with the LSP label as the outer label and the PW label as the inner one.
sections.plainLanguage: The sub-TLV is a name tag on the test message. It says which group it belongs to and which router started it, so the far end knows what to check.

sections.title: Encapsulating the Echo Request
sections.content:
After the MPLS label stack, the echo request is wrapped in one of two options.

  • The Generic Associated Channel Label (GAL) from RFC 6426, followed by an IPv4 (0x0021) or IPv6 (0x0057) type Associated Channel Header (ACH) from RFC 4385.
  • A PW ACH from RFC 4385.

To ensure interoperability, implementations of this document MUST support both encapsulations.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two kinds of envelope the test message can go in. Every router has to know how to open both, so they can all read each other's mail.

sections.title: How a P2MP PW Ping Runs
sections.content:
The RFC's example has a P2MP PW called PW1 from Root PE R-PE1 to Leaf PEs L-PE2, L-PE3 and L-PE4. The transport LSP can be an mLDP P2MP MPLS LSP or a P2MP TE tunnel.

To check connectivity, the operator starts an LSP Ping echo request at R-PE1 with the P2MP Pseudowire sub-TLV in the Target FEC Stack TLV. For an Inclusive tree the label stack is either {P2MP LSP label, GAL} with an IPv4 or IPv6 ACH, or {P2MP LSP label} with a PW ACH. For an Aggregate Inclusive tree the upstream assigned PW label is added after the LSP label.

Intermediate P routers swap labels and replicate the packet based on the incoming LSP label. The L-PEs use the GAL and ACH, or the PW ACH, to recognize an OAM packet. They then check the sub-TLV as described in Section 4.4 of RFC 8029 and reply under the rules of that document.

Echo replies are controlled using RFC 6425. The Echo Jitter TLV (Section 3.3) helps prevent congestion of replies, and the Node Address P2MP Responder Identifier TLV (Section 3.2) can limit the reply to a single L-PE. The RFC says these procedures should be applied.
sections.plainLanguage: The root sends a test message down the branching pipe. Each pipe end opens it, checks it is meant for them and answers back. Special rules stop everyone answering at once.

sections.title: IANA Registration and Security
sections.content:
IANA assigned a new sub-TLV type from the "Sub-TLVs for TLV Types 1, 16, and 21" sub-registry in the MPLS LSPs Ping Parameters registry. The value is 37, named P2MP Pseudowire, and it sits inside the Target FEC Stack TLV (TLV Type 1) from RFC 8029.

On security, the RFC says the proposal does not introduce any new security considerations beyond those that already apply to RFC 6425.
sections.plainLanguage: The new name tag got an official number, 37, in the big list of tags. It is no riskier than the pings that already existed.

fields.name: AGI Type
fields.desc: Type of the Attachment Group Identifier.

fields.name: AGI Value
fields.desc: Variable length; identifies the VPLS instance. Drawn as a variable field.

fields.name: IP Addr Len
fields.desc: Length of the address; determines IPv4 or IPv6.

fields.name: Originating Router's IP Addr
fields.desc: Variable length; IPv4 or IPv6 address of the P2MP PW root. Drawn as a variable field.
